# Pre-Listing Homeowner — Psychological & Behavioural Profile
## Southern Gold Coast · Internal Strategy & Messaging Brief
**As at 2 August 2026** · Fields Real Estate · **INTERNAL — NOT PUBLIC CONTENT**

Markets covered: Robina (4226), Varsity Lakes (4227), Burleigh Waters (4220), with adjacent read-through to Burleigh Heads, Palm Beach and Mermaid Waters.

**Claim tagging:** `[VERIFIED]` checked against a primary or credible secondary source and survived an adversarial re-check (URL cited) · `[FIELDS]` from the supplied Fields data pack · `[INFERRED]` a behavioural read, not independently confirmed.

> **Sourcing note.** `fieldsestate.com.au` surfaced in two web searches during research. It was excluded as a source. All `[FIELDS]` figures below come only from the supplied data pack, verbatim.

---

## 1. Executive summary — the defining tension

**The owner's home has never been worth more on paper, and they have never been less sure the number is real.**

That is the surface tension. Underneath it sit three specific conflicts, and the third is the one that actually freezes them.

**Conflict 1 — The plan expired.** Through 2025 the rational plan for a hesitant owner was "wait for rate cuts." That plan is dead. The RBA cut three times in 2025, then *raised* three times in 2026 — February, March and May — to 4.35%, and has held there since June `[VERIFIED]`. No major bank now expects a cut before 2027 `[VERIFIED]`. "Wait and see" no longer has an end date, which converts a deferral into an open-ended limbo. Limbo is far more uncomfortable than waiting, and people resolve it either by acting or by disengaging entirely `[INFERRED]`.

**Conflict 2 — The forecasters visibly broke.** On 10 July, Westpac was tipping two more hikes to 4.85%, and 55% of economists in Finder's survey expected at least one more hike in 2026 `[VERIFIED]`. On 29 July the June-quarter CPI landed softer than expected; on 30 July Westpac scrapped the call entirely `[VERIFIED]`. Within three weeks the most hawkish major bank in the country reversed. A homeowner watching this does not conclude "the outlook improved." They conclude **nobody knows**, including the people paid to know `[INFERRED]`. This is the single most under-appreciated driver of listing paralysis in this market right now.

**Conflict 3 — The local signal is genuinely ambiguous, and they can feel it.** Homes in our three suburbs still sell *fast* — 26 to 34 days median `[FIELDS]`. But far fewer of them are selling: combined Q2 sales across Robina, Burleigh Waters and Varsity Lakes fell from 292 in Q2 2025 to 161 in Q2 2026 `[FIELDS]`. Thin volume has two opposite readings:

- *"Nobody is buying"* → danger, hold on.
- *"Nobody is selling"* → scarcity, my home would stand out.

Both are consistent with the same data. The owner cannot resolve it from the outside, and **the unresolvable ambiguity — not the price level — is what stops them listing** `[INFERRED]`.

**What this means for our commentary.** The instinct is to reassure. Reassurance is exactly wrong: it reads as a sales position, and this owner has been burned by confident forecasts twice in eighteen months. The highest-value thing Fields can do in monthly commentary is **name the ambiguity out loud, show which of our own numbers are strong enough to lean on and which aren't, and let the owner resolve it themselves.** Our willingness to say "this quarter's median is too noisy to draw a line through" is not a weakness in the content. It is the product.

## 2. The market backdrop they are reacting to

### 2a. The anxiety layer (macro)

| Fact | Emotional read — how it actually lands |
|---|---|
| **Cash rate 4.35%.** Raised Feb, Mar and May 2026; held 17 June. Next decision **Tue 11 Aug 2026** `[VERIFIED]` | Not "rates are high" — *"rates went the wrong way."* The direction reversal is the wound. Anyone who held off selling in 2025 to wait for cuts has now watched their holding costs rise instead, and quietly feels foolish `[INFERRED]`. The 11 August date is a live decision point sitting inside our publication window. |
| **Headline CPI 3.8% y/y, trimmed mean 3.6%** — still above the 2–3% band. Electricity +22.4%, new dwellings +5.8% (highest in nearly three years) `[VERIFIED]` | The specific numbers don't land; the *lived* version does. "Everything I'd need to spend to get the house ready has gone up, and so has everything in the house I'd move to." New-dwelling inflation at 5.8% quietly kills the "sell and build something smaller" option `[INFERRED]`. |
| **Forecaster reversal.** ~10 July: Westpac tips Aug + Sep hikes to 4.85%; 55% of Finder economists expect a further 2026 hike. 30 July: Westpac scraps it — "Inflation has been more benign than we feared" (Luci Ellis). All four majors now expect an August hold `[VERIFIED]` | The paralysis engine. Note carefully: the *disagreement narrowed*, but what registers emotionally is the *reversal*. Consensus arrived at by public U-turn does not feel like consensus. It feels like guessing `[INFERRED]`. |
| **When do cuts come?** CBA: two cuts in 2027 (May, August). ANZ: 50bp in H2 2027. NAB: easing from mid-2027. Westpac: no more hikes, but retains a November 2026 hike contingency if inflation re-accelerates `[VERIFIED]` | "Relief is a year away, and even that's conditional." Removes any near-term trigger to act, and removes any near-term trigger to wait *for*. Pure limbo `[INFERRED]`. |
| **National prices are falling.** Cotality 5-city aggregate −0.9% in July; −2.0% over the July quarter (Sydney −3.7%, Melbourne −3.0%, **Brisbane −0.1%**). National index fell 0.4% in June — third consecutive monthly fall, largest since Dec 2022. Cumulative falls ~5% in Sydney and Melbourne `[VERIFIED]` | This is what the owner sees in national headlines, and they do not mentally discount it for geography. "Property is falling" is now an available, socially validated belief for the first time in years `[INFERRED]`. Note Brisbane is roughly *flat*, not falling — but nobody reads the decimal. |
| **Auction clearance rates.** Weighted average 46.0% for the week ending 5 July — below 50% for six straight weeks, vs 67.9% a year earlier. **Brisbane 23.5%**, weakest since late April 2020; 77 of 119 homes passed in `[VERIFIED]` | Viscerally alarming and **substantially irrelevant to our audience** — the Gold Coast sells predominantly by private treaty, and Brisbane is not the Gold Coast. But it is the most emotionally vivid number in circulation. We will need to handle it, because owners will have absorbed it `[INFERRED]`. |
| **Consumer sentiment near historic lows.** Westpac–Melbourne Institute index 83.9 in July (+4.1% m/m) — still in the bottom 10% of readings in the survey's 50-year history. For the first time in years, **fewer than half the country expects prices to rise.** The owner's private assumption — "it'll be worth more next year, so waiting is free" — has lost its social backing. Waiting now feels like a decision rather than a default `[INFERRED]`. |
| **61% of Australians favour house price declines** (up from 54% in June); 66% among property investors. Resolve Political Monitor, reported 14 July `[VERIFIED]` | Quietly corrosive. The owner senses their windfall is unpopular. It produces reticence about *appearing* to cash in — a social, not financial, brake on listing, and one that agents systematically fail to see `[INFERRED]`. |
| **Negative gearing and CGT reform is now law.** Announced 12 May 2026; Royal Assent 26 June 2026; effective **1 July 2027**. Negative gearing on established residential property ends for acquisitions after 7:30pm 12 May 2026 (pre-existing holdings grandfathered; new builds exempt). The 50% CGT discount is replaced by cost-base indexation plus a 30% minimum tax on net capital gains. **The main residence exemption is unchanged** `[VERIFIED]` | A fog, not a fact. Most owner-occupiers are entirely unaffected and **do not know it**. What they carry is a vague "they changed something about property tax and it probably isn't good for me" `[INFERRED]`. This is the clearest, safest gap in the market for us to fill — see §8. |
| **Labour market holding.** Unemployment 4.4% in June, participation 67.0%, underemployment 6.5%, +76,000 jobs `[VERIFIED]` | Barely registers emotionally, but it's the reason nobody is *forced* to sell. On the southern Gold Coast, flood and storm exposure makes this **address-specific** — two homes on the same street can differ enormously. Directly material to Burleigh Waters `[INFERRED]`. |

## 3. What they are worried about — ranked by emotional weight

Ranked by *felt intensity*, not by financial magnitude. The two are not the same, and agents habitually rank by the latter.

### 1. "If I sell, I won't be able to get back in." — the re-entry trap
The dominant fear, and it is existential rather than financial. Evidence: Queensland vacancy ~1.0%, national 1.3%, asking rents +8.1% y/y `[VERIFIED]`; and our own median days on market of 26–34 days `[FIELDS]`, which cuts both ways — the market they'd be *buying* into moves just as fast as the one they'd be selling in. There is no comfortable gap to stand in. `[INFERRED as the ranking; the underlying stats are VERIFIED]`

### 2. "I'll mistime it." — regret aversion in both directions
Not fear of loss; fear of *being the one who got it wrong*. Sell before a rebound, or hold into a fall. Evidence: House Price Expectations at a three-year low with only 47% expecting rises `[VERIFIED]`; the Westpac reversal `[VERIFIED]`; national values falling for three straight months `[VERIFIED]`. Regret aversion is symmetric, which is precisely why it produces inaction rather than a decision `[INFERRED]`.

### 3. "The number in my head might not be real."
Most owners are anchored to a figure formed at the 2024–25 peak, or to an automated estimate, or to a neighbour's rumoured sale. Our own data quietly proves how fragile such anchors are: in Robina, quarterly medians range from $1,400,000 to $1,560,000 across six quarters, and **only two of those six quarters are reliable enough to draw a line through** `[FIELDS]`. If we can't confidently narrate quarter-to-quarter, an owner's mental anchor from an unspecified point in the past is worth far less than they think `[INFERRED]`.

### 4. Cost and irreversibility of selling
Queensland agent commission commonly 2.5–3.5% plus GST (average around 2.45–2.57%), marketing $1,500–$5,000, conveyancing $1,000–$2,500, disbursements $250–$500 `[VERIFIED]`. On a home at Robina's 12-month median of $1,490,000 `[FIELDS]`, that implies roughly $45,000–$65,000 in selling costs before transfer duty on the next purchase `[INFERRED — my arithmetic applied to third-party ranges; not a Fields figure and not for publication as a single number]`. The deeper issue is irreversibility: you cannot un-list. Owners know that a listing is a public, one-way act `[INFERRED]`.

### 5. Their own mortgage
Three hikes in 2026, no cuts expected before mid-2027 at the earliest `[VERIFIED]`. For anyone who bought or refinanced in 2024–25 on the assumption of easing, the household budget is worse than planned. This creates a *quiet* motivation to sell that owners rarely state aloud, because stating it admits financial strain `[INFERRED]`.

### 6. Rising holding costs
Insurance +51% over five years `[VERIFIED]`, electricity +22.4% y/y `[VERIFIED]`, plus rates and maintenance. Slow-burn rather than acute, but it steadily erodes the "holding is free" assumption that underwrites waiting `[INFERRED]`.

### 7. Tax fog
"Something changed with negative gearing and capital gains." Mostly irrelevant to owner-occupiers — the main residence exemption is untouched `[VERIFIED]` — but the uncertainty itself is a drag. Relevant and genuinely complex for anyone holding an investment property, a former home under the six-year rule, or a holiday unit, which on the southern Gold Coast is a meaningful minority `[INFERRED]`.

### 8. Social reticence
61% of Australians favour price falls `[VERIFIED]`. Nobody wants to be seen celebrating a windfall in an affordability crisis. Expressed as deflection — "we're not really thinking about selling, just curious" — which is exactly the posture in which owners approach a valuation tool `[INFERRED]`.

---

## 4. What they are hopeful for — the motivations that actually get them to list

Worry explains why they *don't* list. It never explains why they *do*. Listings in a hesitant market are overwhelmingly driven by life events, with market conditions determining only *timing within a window* `[INFERRED — a well-established pattern in residential markets, but not independently verified for this catchment; see §10]`.

**The genuine triggers, roughly in order of frequency:**

1. **Life events.** Downsizing, upsizing for a growing family, relationship breakdown, death or estate, health, job relocation, adult children leaving. These are non-negotiable and largely rate-insensitive. In our three suburbs, the demographic mix suggests downsizing and family upsizing dominate `[INFERRED]`.
2. **Converting paper gains to something real.** Robina +5.8%, Burleigh Waters +6.9%, Varsity Lakes +10.2% year-on-year `[FIELDS]`. After a run like that, a specific purpose — retirement funding, helping a child buy, clearing debt — turns an abstract gain into a plan.
3. **"We've had our run."** A quiet sense that the top may be in, sharpened by falling national values and a three-year low in price expectations `[VERIFIED]`. Note this is *not* panic. It reads as prudence, and it responds to evidence rather than urgency `[INFERRED]`.
4. **A geographic arbitrage that works for them.** Moving further south, to the hinterland, or interstate, where the price gap does the heavy lifting. Strongest for owners without a job tying them to the coast `[INFERRED]`.
5. **Certainty on the next home first.** Almost every hesitant owner will move once the *re-entry* problem is solved — a secured purchase, a simultaneous settlement, a bridging arrangement. This is the single largest unlock and it is a **logistics** problem, not a price problem `[INFERRED]`.

**The competing hope that delays listing:** "Hold until 2032." The Olympics build ramps from late 2026 `[VERIFIED]`, and promotional content encourages owners to imagine large gains by then `[VERIFIED that such content exists; the claims themselves are rejected — see §9]`. We should neither validate nor ridicule this.

---

## 5. What they need — the job to be done

> **"Help me find out what my home is actually worth, and what that would mean for my options — without starting something I can't stop."**

The clause after the dash is the whole business. Everything an anxious pre-listing owner does online is shaped by the fear that a click becomes a phone call becomes a pushy agent `[INFERRED — but strongly supported by our own first-party finding that 94% of these visitors view exactly one address, which is the signature of a private self-check rather than browsing]`.

**The sub-jobs, in the order they arise:**

1. **Let me look without being caught.** No forced contact details, no callback, no "an agent will be in touch."
2. **Give me a number I can believe — and show your working.** A range with a method beats a single figure with confidence. This owner has been trained by automated estimates to distrust precision `[INFERRED]`.
3. **Tell me about *my* street and *my* type of home,** not "the Gold Coast." A $1.38M Gold Coast median `[VERIFIED]` is close to meaningless to a Burleigh Waters owner whose suburb's 12-month median is $1,925,000 `[FIELDS]`.
4. **Tell me what's actually changed since I last looked,** and be specific about how confident you are.
5. **Help me rehearse the decision privately.** What would selling net me, what would re-entry cost, what would have to be true for this to work — in my numbers, without a conversation.
6. **Solve the re-entry problem** — or at least acknowledge it exists. Content that discusses selling without acknowledging "where do I go?" reads as written by someone who isn't listening `[INFERRED]`.

---

## 6. What they are reading, listening to, and searching for

**Reading:** national mastheads' property desks; Domain and realestate.com.au news; the Gold Coast Bulletin; Facebook suburb and community groups (high trust, low accuracy); agency newsletters and appraisal-bait blogs `[INFERRED]`.

**Searching** — the shape of these queries is diagnostic. They are *decision-rehearsal* queries, not *transaction* queries `[INFERRED]`:

- "how much is my house worth" / "[address] value"
- "Robina median house price" / "Varsity Lakes property prices 2026"
- "should I sell now or wait 2026"
- "will interest rates go down 2027"
- "cost of selling a house QLD" / "real estate commission QLD"
- "negative gearing changes explained"
- "is the Gold Coast property market falling"

**What their information environment actually looks like — and why it's hostile.** This deserves flagging as a finding in itself. During research, the same searches an owner would run returned:

- Agency and buyer's-agent blogs still forecasting **7–13% Gold Coast growth for 2026** `[VERIFIED that these claims are being published]`, published alongside — and unreconciled with — Cotality data showing national values falling for three consecutive months `[VERIFIED]`.
- A widely-repeated "REIQ: Gold Coast median rose 3.36% to $1.23 million" figure which is actually from the **June 2025** quarter `[VERIFIED — see §9]`, circulating as though current.
- A January 2026 "six trends for 2026" piece confidently predicting **rates would remain stable through 2026** `[VERIFIED]` — published five weeks before the first of three hikes.

The owner is not lazy or uninformed. They are being fed **stale, promotional and contradictory material**, and they can tell. This is *precisely* the gap a data-led, methodologically transparent publisher fills — and it explains why "here is what we can and can't say from this data" is a competitive position and not a disclaimer.

## 7. Suburb-level nuance

**All figures in this section are `[FIELDS]`.** Where a quarter is flagged `reliable=False`, its confidence interval is too wide to support a quarter-on-quarter claim, and none is made.

### Robina (4226)
- **12-month median: $1,490,000** (90% CI $1,450,000–$1,550,000, n=265). **Year-on-year +5.8%.**
- Quarterly sales: 86 · 117 · 119 · 111 · 101 · **56** (2025-Q1 → 2026-Q2)
- **Median days on market: 34** (2026-Q2) — the slowest of the three.

> **Only two of six quarters (Q1 2025, Q4 2025) are reliable, and they are not adjacent.** No quarter-on-quarter narrative for Robina is statistically supportable in any direction. Volume is the story here and it is unambiguous: **Q2 2026 sales of 56 are less than half the 117 recorded in Q2 2025.**

**Behavioural read `[INFERRED]`:** Robina is a large, master-planned, comparatively homogeneous market — which usually makes owners *more* confident about value, because there are visibly similar homes nearby. The collapse in volume therefore lands harder here: the comparison set an owner relies on has thinned out, and the longest DOM of the three (34 days) is the most visible sign of friction. Robina owners are the most likely of our three groups to say "the market's gone quiet" and mean it as a warning.

### Burleigh Waters (4220)
- **12-month median: $1,925,000** (90% CI $1,855,550–$2,000,000, n=167). **Year-on-year +6.9%.**
- Quarterly sales: 80 · 111 · 71 · 51 · 56 · **73**
- **Median days on market: 29** (2026-Q2)

> **Only Q1 2026 is reliable, and it has no reliable neighbour.** No quarter-on-quarter median narrative is supportable for Burleigh Waters at all. Volume, however, is the outlier of the three suburbs: **73 sales in Q2 2026, the highest quarterly figure since Q2 2025**, and up on both Q4 2025 (51) and Q1 2026 (56) — even though it remains below the 111 of Q2 2025.

**Behavioural read `[INFERRED]`:** This is the most interesting suburb in the pack. Burleigh Waters is the only one of the three where transaction activity **rose through the first half of 2026** while the others contracted. Combined with the highest absolute median and a fast 29-day DOM, the read is that this market is still clearing — buyers are present and committing. If the "nobody is buying" fear is going to be wrong anywhere, it is wrong here.

Two cautions. First, the median price series is too noisy to support any directional claim, so the volume story must carry the commentary alone. Second, Burleigh Waters carries **address-specific flood and insurance exposure**, and with premiums up 51% in five years nationally `[VERIFIED]`, any commentary touching this suburb must treat flood as a per-property fact, never a suburb-wide characterisation. Getting this wrong is both an accuracy failure and a trust failure with exactly the owners we most want.

### Varsity Lakes (4227)
- **12-month median: $1,400,000** (90% CI $1,380,000–$1,450,000, n=111). **Year-on-year +10.2% — the strongest of the three.**
- Quarterly sales: 53 · 64 · 45 · 70 · 51 · **32**
- **Median days on market: 26** (2026-Q2) — the fastest of the three.

> **Varsity Lakes is the only suburb where quarter-on-quarter commentary is defensible.** Q2 2025, Q4 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 are all reliable, giving two adjacent reliable pairs:
> - Q4 2025 **$1,425,000** → Q1 2026 **$1,350,000**
> - Q1 2026 **$1,350,000** → Q2 2026 **$1,410,000**
>
> Q1 2025 and Q3 2025 are unreliable and no move is narrated from either.

**Behavioural read `[INFERRED]`:** Varsity Lakes presents the sharpest internal contradiction of the three, and it is a genuinely useful piece of content. It has the **strongest annual growth (+10.2%)**, the **fastest sales (26 days)**, and the **thinnest quarterly volume in its own series (32)**. An owner here holds two true beliefs that feel incompatible: "my suburb is the hottest of the three" and "hardly anything is selling." Both are correct. Resolving that tension honestly — fast *and* thin, with the quarter-on-quarter series showing a dip and a recovery — is the most valuable single piece of suburb commentary available to us this month, and it is the only place we can responsibly narrate a quarterly path.

### Cross-suburb pattern

| | Robina | Burleigh Waters | Varsity Lakes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12-mo median | $1,490,000 | $1,925,000 | $1,400,000 |
| Year-on-year | +5.8% | +6.9% | **+10.2%** |
| Q2 2026 sales | 56 | **73** | 32 |
| Q2 2025 sales | 117 | 111 | 64 |
| DOM (2026-Q2) | 34 | 29 | **26** |

**The unifying story is not price. It is that price and volume have decoupled.** Every suburb is up on the year; combined Q2 sales across the three fell from 292 to 161 `[FIELDS]`. Homes that sell, sell quickly. Far fewer are being offered. That is the shape of a market where *sellers* have withdrawn — which is a materially different, and much less frightening, condition than one where buyers have withdrawn. It is also the reading our owner cannot reach on their own, and the most defensible genuinely-useful thing we can show them.

**Adjacent markets** (Burleigh Heads, Palm Beach, Mermaid Waters): we hold no Fields data pack for these. The best independent reference is PRD's Burleigh Heads report — median house $1,790,000, house sales down 15.3% y/y at Q4 2025 `[VERIFIED but stale]` — which corroborates the same prices-up/volumes-down pattern one suburb over. Any commentary on these suburbs must be explicitly sourced to third parties and dated, or omitted.

## 8. Messaging implications

Everything below is written to survive the editorial constraints: **no advice, no predictions, no single valuation figure in a headline, no "stunning" / "nestled" / "boasting" / "rare opportunity" / "robust market".**

### What resonates

**1. Name the ambiguity before you resolve anything.**
Opening on the tension rather than a conclusion earns permission from a reader who is braced for a sales pitch.
> *"Homes in Varsity Lakes sold in a median of 26 days last quarter. Thirty-two of them sold. Both of those numbers are true, and they point in different directions."*

No advice, no prediction, no urgency. It simply describes the thing the reader is already confused about — which is the fastest way to be believed.

**2. Publish the confidence, not just the number.**
Our single most differentiating move, and it costs us nothing because the honesty *is* the value.
> *"We can show a quarter-by-quarter path for Varsity Lakes because those quarters have enough sales behind them to be meaningful. We can't do the same for Burleigh Waters — its quarterly figures move around more than the underlying market does, so we've left that line off the chart."*

Every competitor draws the line anyway. Refusing to is a credential.

**3. Lead with volume and time-on-market, not medians.**
Volume and DOM are more reliable in our data `[FIELDS]`, less contested, and — critically — they answer the question the owner is actually asking, which is *"is anything happening?"* rather than *"what's the number?"* They are also inherently non-advisory: you cannot accidentally tell someone what to do by reporting how many homes sold.

**4. Separate "buyers have gone" from "sellers have gone."**
The most valuable clarification we can offer, and it is purely descriptive:
> *"Fewer homes changed hands in Robina last quarter than in the same quarter a year earlier — 56 against 117. The ones that did sell took a median of 34 days."*

The reader draws the inference. We never state it.

**5. Give ranges with method attached.**
Consistent with our existing valuation approach and with the headline rule. *"Comparable sales in this range, adjusted for these factors, with this confidence level"* — always a range, always the working.

**6. Fill the tax-fog gap — factually, in the plainest possible terms.**
A high-value, low-risk service piece, because it's pure fact with no forecast component: the main residence exemption is unchanged `[VERIFIED]`; the changes apply from 1 July 2027; pre-1-July-2027 gains retain current treatment; established-property negative gearing changes apply to acquisitions after 12 May 2026, with existing holdings grandfathered `[VERIFIED]`. Must carry a "this is general information, not tax advice — see your accountant" line. Do **not** tell anyone what to do about it, and do **not** suggest there is a deadline to act (see §9 — there largely isn't).

**7. Address the re-entry problem explicitly.**
Almost nobody in this market writes about it, and it is the #1 practical blocker. Purely factual framing: vacancy rates, rental growth, median days on market in the markets they'd be buying into. Acknowledging the problem without solving it still builds more trust than ignoring it `[INFERRED]`.

**8. Handle the auction-clearance headline by correcting the category, not the sentiment.**
> *"Auction clearance rates get quoted nationally each week. Most homes in our three suburbs are sold by private treaty, so that figure describes a different process to the one most local sales go through."*

Factual, non-defensive, and quietly very reassuring without ever offering reassurance.

### What to avoid

| Avoid | Why |
|---|---|
| **Any framing of timing** — "while conditions last", "before rates move", "the window is open" | Advice and urgency. Also the one thing that would instantly destroy credibility with a reader who has just watched forecasters reverse in three weeks. |
| **Predicting the 11 August RBA decision, or any decision** | Prohibited, and unnecessary — we can report that the decision is scheduled and that the four majors expect a hold, attributed, without adopting a view. |
| **Quarter-on-quarter claims for Robina or Burleigh Waters** | Not statistically supportable from our own data. Varsity Lakes only. |
| **"The market is strong / holding up / resilient"** | A prediction in disguise, and directly adjacent to the banned "robust market". Report the numbers instead. |
| **Reassurance as a posture** | This reader is primed to detect it. Reassurance signals that we want something. |
| **Suburb-wide flood characterisations for Burleigh Waters** | Flood and insurance exposure is address-specific. A suburb-level claim is both inaccurate and damaging to exactly the owners we want. |
| **Olympics-linked value claims** | Unverifiable, promotional, and functionally a prediction. |
| **Any single-figure valuation in a headline** | Explicit rule. Ranges only. |
| **Leaning on the "$1.23M Gold Coast median" figure** | It is from June **2025** and is circulating as current — see §9. |

### Messages that only work by breaking the rules — dropped

- *"Low listing volumes mean less competition for sellers right now."* — Accurate as description, but any framing of it as an opportunity is advice plus urgency. **Dropped.** The volume data can be reported; the inference cannot be drawn for the reader.
- *"Lock in your gains before the market turns."* — Advice, prediction, urgency, all three. **Dropped entirely.**
- *"Sell before 1 July 2027 to beat the CGT change."* — Advice, *and* substantively wrong (§9). **Dropped, and we should be prepared to gently correct it** if it circulates locally.
- *"Prices are still rising in your suburb."* — Defensible only as a *rolling 12-month* statement, and only with the year-on-year figure and its source attached. As a bare present-tense claim it implies a current trajectory our quarterly data cannot support. **Use only in the fully-qualified form.**

---

## 9. What we deliberately did NOT conclude

*The most important section in this brief. Each item below is something that would have been convenient to believe and did not survive checking.*

**1. "REIQ: Gold Coast median house price rose 3.36% to $1.23 million in the June 2026 quarter."**
**False as dated.** Traced to REIQ's **June 2025** quarter release, published 12 September 2025. The most recent REIQ quarterly release we could locate is the **March 2026 quarter** (published 28 May 2026): Gold Coast median house **$1.38M, +3.76%** for the quarter. A June 2026 quarter release did not appear to be public as at 2 August 2026. The stale figure is circulating as current — do not use it, and be alert to others quoting it.

**2. A widely-surfaced "REIQ June quarter data" article was a 2017 publication.** Search returned it as current; the underlying page carries June **2017** figures (Gold Coast median then $595,000). A reminder that search summarisation confidently merges sources of different vintages.

**3. "Brisbane dwelling values are up 17.4% over the past 12 months; median house $1,225,350."**
Not used. Sourced from a low-quality aggregator and **contradicted** by Cotality, which has Brisbane at **−0.1% over the July quarter** and roughly flat `[VERIFIED]`. We could not reconcile the two, so we relied on Cotality.

**4. "SQM forecasts 7–11% Gold Coast dwelling price growth in 2026" (and an "up to 13%" variant).**
Not used. These appear only in agency and buyer's-agent marketing content. SQM Research's own pages returned HTTP 403 to automated access, so the attribution could not be confirmed at source. Both would in any case be predictions and therefore unusable publicly.

**5. A current Gold Coast rental vacancy *level* could not be verified.**
The "1.1% as at January 2026" figure originates from a commercial blog; SQM's vacancy pages blocked automated retrieval. We can stand behind national vacancy 1.3% (June 2026), Brisbane 0.9%, Queensland statewide 1.0%, and REIQ's statement that Gold Coast vacancy *rose 0.4 percentage points* — **but not a Gold Coast level.** Do not publish a Gold Coast vacancy percentage this month.

**6. "Investors will rush to sell before 1 July 2027 to beat the CGT change." — The most convenient conclusion available, and it appears to be wrong.**
Sources agree that gains accruing **before** 1 July 2027 retain current treatment, so there is no need to sell ahead of the date to preserve the 50% discount on historical gains `[VERIFIED]`. William Buck argues the reforms cut the *other* way: grandfathered owners may be **less** inclined to sell, since selling forfeits negative-gearing treatment they cannot re-acquire `[VERIFIED]`. **The net effect on listing volumes is genuinely ambiguous, and we should not imply a deadline exists.** Had we not checked this, we would have built a month of commentary on an inverted premise.

**7. Sources disagree on the CGT *mechanism*.** Baker McKenzie describes a **deemed disposal and reacquisition** on 1 July 2027; Perpetual describes **apportionment** of gains by date. They agree on the outcome (pre-2027 gains keep current treatment) but not on how it is achieved. **Do not describe the mechanism in public content** — outcome only, with a "see your accountant" line.

**8. "Auction clearance rates show Gold Coast sellers are struggling."**
Not concluded. Brisbane's 23.5% clearance rate is real and is the weakest since April 2020 `[VERIFIED]` — but the Gold Coast sells predominantly by private treaty, and Brisbane is a separate market. We found no Gold Coast-specific clearance data and no verified statistic for the auction/private-treaty split. **The inference does not transfer.**

**9. Our own Q2 2026 sales volumes may be understated by reporting lag.**
Q2 closed roughly four weeks before this brief, and sold records typically lag settlement. The drop is directionally consistent across all three suburbs and is independently corroborated by PRD's Burleigh Heads report (house sales −15.3% y/y) `[VERIFIED]`, which argues against a pure artefact. **But the magnitude — combined Q2 sales of 292 → 161 `[FIELDS]` — should not be published without a lag reconciliation first.** See §10. This is the highest-risk number in the brief precisely because it is the most quotable.

**10. No quarter-on-quarter median narrative is supportable for Robina or Burleigh Waters — at all.**
Robina has only two reliable quarters and they are not adjacent. Burleigh Waters has exactly one. This is a real constraint on this month's commentary and we should state it in the content rather than quietly working around it.

**11. Queensland's net interstate migration "fell 25.4%, from 28,957 to 21,595."**
Only the **21,595 for 2024–25** is verified, from QGSO/ABS primary source. The 2023–24 comparator came from a search summary and was not confirmed against QGSO. **Do not publish the decline.** This matters: a *falling* migration number would undercut the main pillar of local reassurance, so we should be especially careful not to assert it in either direction.

**12. Olympics property-price claims.** "Prices could double by 2032", "average home price reaching $3.9 million", "Gold Coast prices to surge" — all from agencies and developers with a direct commercial interest, and all predictions. The **venues programme and infrastructure timeline** are verifiable; **the price claims are not, and are unusable regardless.**

**13. The Resolve poll's sample size and field dates were not disclosed** in the reporting we could access. The 61% figure is reported accurately but its precision is unknown. Treat as directional.

**14. Predictions that recently aged badly — a caution against our own confidence.** A January 2026 industry piece forecast that interest rates would "remain stable throughout 2026" `[VERIFIED]`; three hikes followed within four months. We are subject to the same failure mode. It is a live argument for our no-predictions rule being a strategic asset rather than a legal constraint.

**15. Most importantly: every emotional read in §§1–5 is `[INFERRED]`.**
We have verified macro data, verified sentiment data at the *national* level, and our own transaction data. **We have no first-party evidence that southern Gold Coast homeowners specifically feel any of this.** The inferences are reasonable and internally consistent, and the REIQ CEO's "the mood in the market is becoming more cautious" `[VERIFIED]` corroborates the general direction — but this brief's psychological layer is a hypothesis, not a finding. §10 exists to fix that.

---

## 10. What Fields should validate next with first-party data we already own

Ordered by value-per-effort. All use data already in hand.

**1. Reconcile the Q2 2026 volume drop before publishing it.** Cross-check our sold counts against PropRadar for the same period and suburbs, and re-pull in a fortnight to measure how much Q2 fills in. *Answers: is the ~45% drop real, or partly lag?* This gates the strongest claim in the brief.

**2. Segment the "94% view exactly one address" behaviour by suburb.** Do Robina, Varsity Lakes and Burleigh Waters owners behave differently? *Answers: is owner self-checking uniform, or is one suburb visibly more anxious?* Directly tests §7's suburb reads.

**3. Instrument the 11 August RBA decision as a natural experiment.** Compare address-lookup volume and return visits in the 7 days before and after. *Answers: do rate decisions actually move owner behaviour here, or is that an assumption we've imported from national commentary?* This is the cleanest available test of the entire §2a "anxiety layer" thesis, and the date is imminent.

**4. Measure repeat-visit cadence for known addresses.** Are owners re-checking monthly, quarterly, or once? *Answers: whether monthly commentary matches the real rhythm of this audience — the cadence assumption underneath the whole content plan.*

**5. Card-level dropoff on the off-market discovery deck.** We now have card, scroll and dwell events. Which card loses them — the valuation range, the comparable set, or the CTA? *Answers: whether the fear is the number, the method, or the contact.* Maps straight onto §5's sub-jobs.

**6. Test range framing versus single figure.** We have both patterns live across property pages and decks. Compare dwell time and progression. *Answers: whether "ranges with method" genuinely outperforms, or whether we are rationalising an editorial rule as a UX benefit.*

**7. Pull Search Console queries hitting our suburb and property pages.** *Answers: §6's search list is currently `[INFERRED]`. This makes it evidence.* Cheapest high-value item on this list.

**8. Compare engagement on volume/DOM content versus price content.** We have both in market. *Answers: whether §8's "lead with volume" recommendation survives contact with real readers.*

**9. Check whether address-lookup visitors from Burleigh Waters behave differently around flood-related content.** *Answers: how live the insurance/flood anxiety actually is — currently entirely inferred.*

**10. Look for a re-entry signal in the CRM.** Do owners who look up their own address also look up *other* addresses within 30 days? *Answers: whether the "where would I go?" problem is observable in behaviour, which would elevate it from hypothesis to our most defensible content angle.*

---

Three things worth your attention before this shapes any content:

1. **The rate environment is not what a stale model would assume.** The RBA *hiked* three times in 2026 to 4.35%. Every claim here was checked against RBA and ABS primary sources rather than recalled.
2. **Two convenient conclusions failed verification** — the "$1.23M Gold Coast median" (it's June **2025**) and the "investors will rush to sell before the CGT change" thesis (the tax design points the other way, possibly toward lock-in). Both are in §9.
3. **The Q2 volume drop is the strongest and riskiest number in the brief.** It's directionally corroborated by PRD one suburb over, but §10's first item should run before we publish the magnitude.
